High heating oil prices are a potent issue in northern states that depend on the fuel like Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska, which have competitive Senate races on November 3 that could determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans maintain control of Congress, according to Reuters interviews with 15 voters, candidates and strategists. Democratic candidates have sought to tie the higher costs to Trump's war with Iran, which has disrupted global diesel supplies. The shortage drove prices for diesel, which is similar to heating oil, to a record high above $6.50 a gallon, making groceries and consumer staples more expensive. Reuters was first to report this week that the US Energy Department [USN:L1N46700H TEXT:"released"] heating oil from reserves in the Northeast. When asked about criticism that Trump's policies have led to soaring heating oil costs that could make Republicans vulnerable, the White House pointed to that fuel release, a move an analyst said was unlikely to affect prices. Heating oil prices have climbed above $6 per gallon nationally, up from about $3.50 a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration. The costs are a headwind for Republicans, said Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. "The party in power is held responsible for things like that, and it’s so clearly Trump’s fault because of this Iran war." Nearly 80% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame"] Trump policies for higher costs including energy, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. In New Hampshire, where 43% of residents use heating oil, Pappas said energy dominates voters' concerns as he challenges Republican John Sununu. "Energy costs and heating oil prices are the beginning and end of every conversation I'm having on the campaign trail," Pappas said. Sununu’s campaign did not respond to several requests for comment. ALASKA EVEN HIGHER In Alaska, where roughly 30% of residents rely on heating oil, the issue has surfaced in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has campaigned on lowering energy costs. In remote Alaska communities, fuel is often shipped long distances. Diesel also generates electricity and powers transportation, pushing up the cost of goods and services. In the Yukon River community of St. Mary's, Mayor Sven Paukan said heating fuel has risen to about $10 per gallon, roughly $2 more than last year. "It's pretty difficult to heat homes nowadays," Paukan said. Sullivan said he supports a "temporary pause of American diesel exports," a policy [USN:SPN45A01C TEXT:"Trump has considered"]. A Peltola spokesperson said the Iran war had helped drive up heating fuel, gasoline and grocery costs in Alaska. Sullivan has said he supports the war but that it should end soon, and this week he encouraged Alaska fishermen to apply for a new $8 billion Trump administration [USN:SPN4650BH TEXT:"program"] to offset diesel costs for farmers. Suzanne Downing, former communications director for the Alaska Republican Party, said heating oil is a concern for Republicans. "Many people in Fairbanks ... pay more in the wintertime for their fuel bill than they do for their mortgage," she said. "The Iran war is being blamed for this." MAINE 'DOUBLE WHAMMY' In Maine, where 54% of homes use heating oil, rising fuel costs have featured in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson. The costs are even higher for fishermen and farmers who use diesel to power their motors and warm homes with oil. "For them, it really is a double whammy," said Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine. "Folks who probably have the lowest incomes are the ones who are facing the highest energy costs," said Scott Thistle, spokesperson for MaineHousing, the public housing authority, adding older housing stock and mobile homes are costlier to heat. Gerry Cushman, a fifth-generation lobsterman from Port Clyde, said fishermen were already facing fluctuating prices for their catches. But Cushman said he plans to support Collins, the Republican, arguing that her seniority and influence outweigh voters' frustrations. "If you're a senior senator and you're head of (Senate Committee on Appropriations), you can get more done than a freshman senator,” he said. Collins said after initially supporting the war she has voted several times to bring it to an end. She also pushed the US government to speed the release of $38 million for Maine from the $4 billion federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and urged Trump to tap the heating oil reserve. That's not enough for Maine lobsterman Dave Cousens of South Thomaston, who plans to vote for Jackson. Cousens blamed high energy costs on Trump's Iran war and said he will be forced to forgo a Florida vacation. "He picked a fight with the wrong country, and we're all paying for it."

item.title: Divided over Israel, Detroit Democrats unite on rising costs for midterm elections
item.description: It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.
item.dc:creator: Heather Schlitz
item.content:encoded: It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present. Broadnax, a 42-year-old single mother of four in Detroit, said soaring gas and grocery prices left little money to pay the bills, let alone buy gifts or throw a birthday party. “It’s hard to tell your kids that you don't have the funds right now to buy them a $3 bag of Skittles,” she said while watching her sons practice with a free basketball team at St. Suzanne Community Resource Center. Ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Broadnax’s concerns are widely shared in Detroit. Jewish, Muslim and Black voters interviewed by Reuters often put affordability ahead of disputes over Israel and Gaza, even as many expressed reservations about Democratic US Senate nominee [USN:L1N4420RK TEXT:"Abdul El-Sayed"]. El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim US senator, faces former congressman Mike Rogers in a competitive race that could help determine control of the Senate. A RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a two-point lead – 48% to 46%. Broadnax has yet to decide who to support, saying she will vote for the candidate most focused on lowering costs. She sometimes skips meals so her children can eat and chooses which bills to pay after gas eats up at least $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day driving for Lyft. “Being a single mom, trying to take care of four boys out here in America now is too hard,” she said. “Whatever candidate whose main focus is affordability – that’s who I’m going with.” But El-Sayed faces resistance from some voters who would ordinarily be inclined to support a Democrat, particularly over Israel. “Both of the candidates have decided that this election is about Abdul,” said Matt Grossmann, a political science professor at Michigan State University. “He needs to win over voters that would normally support the Democratic candidate and are upset with President Trump but might have reservations about him – personal or policy reservations.” El-Sayed’s challenge is not only keeping uneasy Democrats from voting for Rogers, but getting them to vote at all. Some voters told Reuters that opposing Trump made backing Rogers difficult, while concerns about El-Sayed led others to consider sitting out the race. JEWISH VOTERS’ RESERVATIONS Most Jewish voters in Detroit traditionally vote Democratic, but some have deep reservations about El-Sayed over his views on Israel, particularly his response to a March attack on a suburban synagogue. After a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel while more than 100 children were inside, El-Sayed drew backlash when he said “hurt people hurt people" in reference to the attacker. Though El-Sayed later apologized for the comment, he has continued to draw heavy criticism from a community shaken by the attack. Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek said some Jewish men now cover their heads with baseball caps instead of yarmulkes because they fear being targeted if identified as Jews. Starr's synagogue spends twice as much on security measures for its sprawling campus following the attack. Starr and a group of Jewish clergy launched a petition calling for the Democratic Party to agree to a set of “non-negotiable” principles, including acknowledging Israel’s right to exist and Jewish sovereignty in Israel. El-Sayed has not signed the petition or communicated with the group, Starr said. He said he would not vote for the Democratic nominee. “He is hyper-focused on Israel and American supporters of the state of Israel and seemed to be placing an awful lot of blame on Israel for America's problems,” Starr said in his study, where “hurt people help people” yard signs leaned against a wall beside shelves of religious texts. El-Sayed briefly campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has drawn criticism over comments about Israel and American Jews. The association has troubled some voters, while others remain more focused on the cost of living. “I don't love the fact that he campaigned with Hasan Piker during the primary,” said Alicia Chandler, a 47-year-old Jewish Detroit resident and former supporter of El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens. “But it cost me almost $100 to fill my car with gas yesterday.” El-Sayed has repeatedly pledged to protect Jewish people from antisemitism, saying in an August speech after winning the Democratic primary that his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” GAZA AND THE POCKETBOOK In 2024, frustration with the Biden-Harris administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza drove many Arab American and Muslim voters in Michigan away from the Democratic ticket, with some backing the Republican Trump or third-party candidates and others choosing not to vote. At Shibam Coffee, a Yemeni coffeehouse in the Arab-majority city of Dearborn, volunteers wearing “Abdul for Senate” shirts gathered over cardamom coffee, honeycomb bread and sambusas before heading out to canvass. The cafe is popular with young Arab Americans, many of whom now support El-Sayed. Sumayah Dhalai, a 22-year-old senior at Wayne State University who plans to vote for El-Sayed, liked his policy position opposing funding for the Israeli government but said her fears about finding a job and affording rent and groceries were a bigger factor in deciding who to vote for. “The overwhelming majority of us are very scared about graduating because everybody’s telling us that everything sucks,” Dhalai said. “As much as I want to say I'm out here fighting for world peace, I have to ensure my own ability to succeed before I can then turn to focus on everybody else's.” While parts of Detroit have benefited from new investment, others have not, including the neighborhood housing St. Suzanne Community Resource Center, where the median household income is just $36,525 and roughly half the children live in poverty, according to US Census data. “The financial stress is continual,” said Steve Wasko, the director of the center where Broadnax's sons play basketball. “Being able to pay your rent, afford your light bill, pay your mortgage, or pay to have your furnace working sufficiently – these are the most common requests that come through the door."

item.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
item.description: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress. In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks. Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country: TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items. But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses. Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends. The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people. “Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family." RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory. Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday. Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election. Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa. Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine. TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity. But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues. "I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special." The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens. At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty. Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday. Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them. FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods. But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade. “What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran. “They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world. TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic. This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton. At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.” “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said. Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old." Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents. Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton. "Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't." That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

item.title: Kamala Harris returns to US campaign trail with midterms, 2028 in view
item.description: Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Allen
item.content:encoded: Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028. The Democratic Party's unsuccessful [USN:L1N3MD1RL TEXT:"2024"] standard-bearer has made relatively few public appearances this year. But with her party trying to break the Republican hold on Congress on November 3, Harris is rallying in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, a return likely to renew questions about her political future as a crowded field of [USN:L1N41L0MR TEXT:"potential 2028 contenders"] takes shape. Harris kicked off her tour in Las Vegas on Tuesday with a new stump speech attacking what she described as the cruelty of President Donald Trump, mixed with the aspirational aphorisms that have long been her calling card as the first Black and Asian person and first woman to become vice president. She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada's first Black attorney general, who she said would be the "first Black governor west of the Mississippi." "We got a serious fight in front of us," Harris said. "We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration." Like Trump, who is [USN:L1N45X06G TEXT:"jetting around the country"] for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were starkly partisan: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared to 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents. "At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters," said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. "That's what's going on here with her, and frankly with Trump." The day after Las Vegas, Harris led chants of "Mississippi matters!" to a crowd supporting Scott Colom in the city of Columbus. Colom is seeking to become the first Democratic US senator elected in Mississippi since 1982, and polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith. Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: "Never let someone else's limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition," she said. "Let me repeat that." And she did, louder than the first time, drawing cheers from the crowd. UNDECIDED ON 2028 If Harris decides to run again for the White House in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field. But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats: she lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first White House campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began. A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats' chaotic 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign over questions about his health and mental acuity and she replaced him as the nominee. Harris has since called Biden's decision to seek reelection "reckless" in her memoir "107 Days," a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of his support for Israel's war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government's "horrific conduct" and saying the US should have "acted sooner and more forcefully." "All these things will be relitigated," Kamarck said. "What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on." Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of "How the Democrats Lost America," said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost, though voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light. "She has that kind of crossover appeal," Ferson said, "particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home." Her implicit message, he suggested, is "Do you regret staying home?" This month, as she wrapped up an appearance on the "Baby, This Is Keke Palmer" video podcast, Palmer asked her if she would run again. "Oh, girl, come on!" Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. "I haven't decided yet." "But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms," Harris went on. "2028 don't matter if we don't do 2026 right."

item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: Data dreams delayed
item.description: The multi-trillion-dollar data centre boom is running into physical and financial constraints. This week’s update asks: what happens if fewer server farms get built? Plus: the challenge of paying for AI-hungry agents, and who deserves to win the board standoff at India’s Tata.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! This weekly update showcases the best bits of Breakingviews. For full access to everything our columnists have to offer every day, consider taking out a subscription. Subscribe here for you or your team. OPENING LINE “Netflix (NFLX.O) is in danger of starring in a financial version of ‘Squid Game.’ Slowdowns in subscriber and revenue growth, along with its botched $83 billion deal to buy Warner Bros., threaten to leave the pioneering streaming service fighting for its life like the contestants in its most popular show ever.” Read more: [USN:L6N46610R TEXT:"Netflix morphs into same couch potato it mashed"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK The top 20% of Israeli workers bring in 93% of the government’s income-tax revenue. ([USN:L6N4650XE TEXT:"Electoral stakes are high"]) Advanced manufacturing and technology accounted for 40% of China’s GDP growth in the third quarter. ([USN:L4N4620ID TEXT:"Unbalanced on purpose"]) French government interest payments this year will amount to 2.3% of GDP, below Italy’s 3.9%. ([USN:L6N4620Y8 TEXT:"Deficit control is distant"]) Gross margins on EssilorLuxottica’s (ESLX.PA) smart Ray-Bans may be lower than for regular eyewear. ([USN:L6N4670LC TEXT:"Competition is heating up"]) Analyst expectations for Tesla’s (TSLA.O) 2026 operating income have crashed 80% in the past two years. ([USN:L6N467105 TEXT:"SpaceX merger is hard to resist"]) RACK AND RUIN So far, the debate about artificial intelligence data centres has been mostly about the vastness of the boom. Do we really need all these server farms, who will pay for them, and where will they find the electricity to power – and water to cool – vast racks of processors? However, recent market jitters raise a newly urgent question: what happens if fewer data centres get built? Start with some eye-popping numbers. Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School estimates the AI boom will produce 183 gigawatts of data centre capacity in the United States alone by 2032, almost five times the pre-2025 figure. This splurge will cost more than $10 trillion and amount to more than 3.5% of US GDP over the period, making earlier investment crazes like railroads and telecoms look sober by comparison. In the past few weeks, though, this vision has dimmed. Investors are questioning the financial viability of so-called neoclouds, the upstart developers which build data centres under contract for tech giants. Rising borrowing costs have squeezed the margin firms like CoreWeave (CRWV.O) can [USN:L6N46113K TEXT:"earn"] from buying and renting out Nvidia (NVDA.O) chips, casting doubt over future growth. Rival [USN:L6N45V00W TEXT:"Firmus Technologies"] cancelled its initial public offering; other stock sales look doubtful. Technological dreams are also colliding with real-world obstacles. Delays in accessing the electricity grid prompted Microsoft (MSFT.O) to [USN:L6N4650TB TEXT:"walk away"] from a UK lease with neocloud upstart Nscale. Shares in Australia’s NextDC (NXT.AX) crashed after [USN:L6N46808I TEXT:"local opposition"] forced it to shelve a project in Melbourne. Oracle (ORCL.N) previously [USN:L6N45H0NU TEXT:"flagged"] similar problems in New Mexico. Multiple US states have imposed moratoria on new data centre construction. It’s important to keep the problems in context. Nscale’s cancelled project in London had a planned capacity of 50 megawatts. By comparison, Elon Musk this week predicted that SpaceX (SPCX.O) would have at least 13 gigawatts of computing grunt by the end of 2027, up from just 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September. Musk claims his company is being “haunted relentlessly” by tech giants and others seeking server horsepower. SpaceX’s chief financial officer says demand is so strong that its data centre investments are paying for themselves in less than a year. Blackstone (BX.N) President Jon Gray echoed the sentiment, arguing that a squeeze on new construction makes the private equity giant’s completed projects more valuable. Even so, a world with fewer, more expensive AI data centres would force a wholesale recalibration. Chipmakers and other equipment suppliers would have to adapt to lower demand, AI users would be required to recalibrate technology costs, and financiers would need to reconsider their exposures. Rapidly rethinking the scale of a boom this big is bound to cause severe whiplash. CHART OF THE WEEK One reason tech companies need more data centres is to serve AI agents: more than 10 million people have downloaded Meta Platforms’ (META.O) Muse assistant, for example. Digital helpers are heavy users of computing power, burning through 7 times as many tokens as human-led chat prompts. How will the Facebook owner pay for it? [USN:L6N45S0SU TEXT:"Karen Kwok calculates"] that transaction fees and advertising are unlikely to cover the running costs. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS Back in 2021 the investment strategist Richard Bernstein coined the term “Everything Bubble” to describe the exuberant state of markets emerging from the pandemic. Now stocks are flashing familiar warnings: abundant liquidity, frantic trading, and enthusiastic retail investors. On The Big View , I talked to the financial historian and Breakingviews columnist Edward Chancellor about why the “Everything Bubble” has proved so persistent – and why he thinks this market may be the most speculative ever. In the Viewsroom this week, Aimee Donnellan and Jonathan Guilford were joined by Karen Kwok to discuss the market jitters about financing AI infrastructure. They debate whether the damage can be contained, and if trouble in AI’s plumbing could further dent Anthropic’s weakening growth. PARTING SHOT For sheer corporate drama, the boardroom struggle over Tata Sons is hard to beat. In one corner is N. Chandrasekaran, the chair of India’s oldest conglomerate. In the other is Noel Tata, the scion of the founding family who chairs Tata Trusts, the group of charities that are the steel-to-software giant’s largest shareholder. There will be painful consequences whoever prevails. But in the end, [USN:L6N4600OF TEXT:"Una Galani argues"], defeat for the executive known as Chandra would mainly hurt the group and its 26 listed companies. If Noel Tata is thwarted it would be a setback for shareholder rights across India. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . Follow Peter Thal Larsen on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: Barcelona like a local
item.description: Our correspondent's guide to sun-kissed plazas, tapas and beach escapes
item.dc:creator: Joan Faus
item.content:encoded:
REUTERS/Illustration/Olivia Waller I was born and raised in Barcelona and, after living abroad for about 10 years, returned in 2019 to cover politics, migration, and other topics from the city, most recently for Reuters. My hometown had changed quite a lot in that time. Barcelona was much more racially diverse and packed with tourists than when I was a kid. Coming home made me realize what I had missed the most living outside of Spain, besides friends and family: the sun, quaint pedestrianized squares, and the Mediterranean Sea. The city's spirit was knocked by deadly attacks in 2017 and the fallout of Catalonia's failed independence bid , which led scores of companies to move their headquarters. But it bounced back with energy. It has a strong startup scene and quality of life that, paired with the boom in remote working, has lured increasing numbers of foreigners. That has put pressure on prices and has not been welcomed by everyone. But in its long-standing competition with Spain's capital city, Madrid — in politics, business and, of course, soccer — Barcelona is brimming with confidence. People sit at outdoor restaurants along a beachfront. REUTERS/Nacho Doce People sit at a bar terrace next to Santa Maria del Mar in the Born neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea A drone view of the Basilica Sagrada Familia, designed by Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi. REUTERS/Guillermo Martinez Members of the Castellers del Poble Sec, Castellers de Barcelona, Castellers de la Sagrada Familia and Castellers de Sarria form a human tower, or "castell", at Barcelona's Sant Jaume square during La Merce festival. REUTERS/Nacho Doce A group of people practice yoga during sunrise at the beach. REUTERS/Bruna Casas A drone view of the Casa Mila, designed by Catalan architect Antoni Gaudi. REUTERS/Guillermo Martinez A boy jumps in the water in la Barceloneta. REUTERS/ Bruna Casas People sit at a bar terrace in Fossar de les Moreres in the Born neighbourhood. REUTERS/ Albert Gea A drone view of the Mapfre Tower and the Hotel Arts. REUTERS/Guillermo Martinez A drone view of the Mapfre Tower, Hotel Arts and the Olympic Port. REUTERS/Guillermo Martinez Tourists walk past a souvenir shop near the Sagrada Familia basilica. REUTERS/Nacho Doce Performers dressed as devils hold sticks spewing fire sparks during the traditional "Correfoc" (fire run) as part of the La Merce festival, which celebrates Barcelona's patron saint. REUTERS/Nacho Doce People walk along a narrow street in the Born neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea People sit at a bar terrace on Consell de Cent street in the Eixample neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea A woman goes up the stairs at the Gabriel Garcia Marquez Library in the Sant Marti neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea A person walks past Abissinia restaurant in the Gracia neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea People walk past Anita Gelato at Plaza de la Vila de Gracia square in the Gracia neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea People dance in Plaza de la Vila de Gracia square in the Gracia neighbourhood. REUTERS/Albert Gea A drone view of Somorrostro beach. REUTERS/Guillermo Martinez Here's how to visit the Catalan capital like a local: The way around: Barcelona has a very comprehensive public transport system that can take you to most places in less than half an hour. It is also a very walkable city. Cycling is very much on the rise thanks to the installation of cycling paths in recent decades. Still, many locals prefer to get around using small motorcycles, given the city's compactness, hilly neighbourhoods and pleasant weather. There are several apps you can use to rent motorcycles, including Cooltra and Yego , which charge per ride. People watching: Barcelona has loads of cute pedestrianized plazas, including Plaça Virreina or Plaça de la Vila, both in the Gràcia neighbourhood. Having breakfast, tapas or a drink in one of these squares provides a window into Spanish social life, where everyone from young children to elders spends their time against the backdrop of soothing street music. What to eat: As the most-visited Spanish city by foreigners, Barcelona has plenty of tourist traps. But there are several amazing and award-winning restaurants, if you know where to look. A hidden gem for great food quality and atmosphere is Les Filles Cafe , offering fusion cuisine and brunches served in a small, lush oasis in a Gràcia courtyard. In the same neighbourhood, you can go for Ethiopian food at the authentic Abissinia . For a refreshing Gilda (olive, anchovy and pepper served on a toothpick) and other good Spanish tapas like cod tortilla, Dalt de Tot in the Sant Gervasi neighbourhood is a safe bet. For something sweet, Barcelona has a vast array of pastry shops where you can try seasonal traditions, like marzipan-based "panellets" around All Saints' Day on November 1 or "monas," chocolate sculptures served during Easter. If it's cold outside, you can soak "melindros" — light and fluffy sponge fingers that are softer and less oily than churros — in hot chocolate at a "granja," a traditional cafe. To unwind : Compared to other major European cities, Barcelona isn't blessed with many large parks. But there are still plenty of options to unwind and see some greenery. Parc del Guinardó offers amazing views of the city with a fraction of the crowds seen at the nearby Antoni Gaudí-designed Park Güell. The same goes for the Carretera de les Aigües, a long, gravel path that snakes through the foothills of the Collserola mountain range along Barcelona's northern edge and is ideal for running or walking. To address the city's urban density and spurred by the COVID-19 pandemic, Barcelona in 2023 opened a so-called green axis on Consell de Cent, a central and flat street featuring a 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) pedestrianized stretch, ideal for leisurely strolls. To go really off the beaten track, visit the Gabriel García Márquez Library in the working-class Sant Martí neighbourhood. Named in honour of the late Colombian Nobel literature laureate who lived in Barcelona from 1967 to 1975, it specialises in Latin American literature and won an award in 2023 for the best new public library in the world. Its hammocks for reading or napping are certainly a bonus! The hot ticket: Watching a football game at Barcelona's revamped Camp Nou stadium is a deep dive into one of the city's and region's proudest symbols. But it's not cheap: tickets to watch the men's team usually start around €160 ($182) via the club's official website or ticket offices, and are much pricier for the coveted and nerve-racking "El Clásico" game against Real Madrid. The women's team plays at Johan Cruyff Stadium, the club's training complex outside the city, and tickets are much more accessible. General view inside Spotify Camp Nou. REUTERS/Albert Gea FC Barcelona fans inside the stadium before the match against Real Madrid. REUTERS/Albert Gea FC Barcelona's Joao Cancelo in action with Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz. REUTERS/Albert Gea Beach escapes: Barcelona has nine beaches, all of which are easily reached via public transport, and where you can enjoy the Spanish pastime of going to a "chiringuito," a beach bar serving drinks, tapas and fresh seafood. If you're seeking less crowded and more pristine beaches, there are plenty of accessible options outside town. A 30-minute Rodalies commuter train ride takes you to Garraf beach, where some people still live in green and white wooden houses traditionally used by fishermen, and restaurants offer seafood paellas alongside scenic backdrops. People enjoy Cala Treumal beach in Lloret de Mar on the Costa Brava, north of Barcelona, Spain, October 21, 2026. REUTERS/Albert Gea And if you don't mind renting a car, a one-hour drive takes you from Barcelona to the stunning Cala Treumal, a secluded small cove at the start of the Costa Brava, where pine tree-covered hills descend to the azure-coloured sea.

CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population : 1.7 million (5.7 million in the wider metropolitan area) Price of a coffee: About €1.50 ($1.70) for an espresso ("café solo"). In Spain, if you ask for iced coffee ("café con hielo") you will get hot coffee and a separate glass with ice, for you to assemble yourself — much to the dismay of sophisticated coffee connoisseurs or foreigners. Price of ice cream: €4 ($4.50) for a scoop of gelato from AMMA Gelato in Gràcia’s Virreina square, which has great vegan options. Essential read: There are plentiful books narrating key moments in Barcelona's history, from its time as Barcino during the Roman Empire to its latest transformations. George Orwell's "Homage to Catalonia" (1938), based on the English writer's experience during the Spanish Civil War, takes you to revolutionary Barcelona in the 1930s at a defining historical moment. Spanish novelist Juan Marsé's 1966 "Últimas tardes con Teresa" (Last Evenings with Teresa) depicts class divisions and youthful dreams during General Francisco Franco's 1939-1975 dictatorship. And the 2006 bestseller "La Catedral del Mar" (Cathedral of the Sea) from Ildefonso Falcones is set in the city during the construction of the Santa Maria del Mar church in the 14th century.

item.title: Chase & Status on the upside of AI for music
item.description: The British electronic music duo Saul Milton and Will Kennard discuss their new album, “Generic Everything,” originality, and the value of individuality in the age of algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Sam Tabahriti
item.content:encoded: Will Kennard and Saul Milton of the English drum and bass duo Chase & Status pose for a photograph in London, Britain, September 30, 2026. REUTERS/Hannah McKay Chase & Status have spent more than two decades chasing the next sound, amassing more than 2 billion streams on Spotify along the way. Their latest album, released earlier this month, “Generic Everything,” is driven by a different concern: the fear that technology is making culture more uniform. The British electronic music duo, Saul Milton (known as Chase) and Will Kennard (Status), say the record emerged from conversations about artificial intelligence, social media and the growing pressure for artists to follow established formulas rather than forge their own path. Still, they reject the idea that AI poses an existential threat to creativity. Speaking to Reuters in London, the pair discuss originality, technological change and why they believe individuality will become more valuable in an age of algorithms. This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity. Your new album is called “Generic Everything.” It's a provocative title for a duo that's spent two decades building a distinctive sound. What does it mean? Kennard: It sounds like an angry statement, but it wasn't really meant that way. When we were making the record, we found the rate of change in technology, the impact of social media and the fast-changing pace of AI really overwhelming and confusing. We spoke to other artists and friends who felt the same. The danger of that was that our own work started to sound a bit lazy and a bit generic. We could see that in other people's work as well. It felt like creativity was being squeezed into a singular space. "Generic Everything" was a phrase we wrote on a whiteboard in the studio. It was a reminder to think differently and not always take the easy route. It became a personal mission to avoid the pitfalls of just sounding like everything else. Which track unlocked the album for you? Was there one song that made everything else make sense? Milton: I think it was less a single track and more a movement away from the record we originally thought we were making. During the process, the sound palette we were working with changed quite dramatically. We moved away from one idea and into a different place. Kennard: "Disgruntled" was probably the moment we realised what we wanted the record to be. It had this guitar-led, punky, live feel that was very different from where we'd been before. That gave us the confidence to push further in that direction with tracks like "Tension". If someone from outside Britain listened to “Generic Everything,” what would they understand about Britain in 2026? Milton: All of our albums are a kaleidoscope into what's happening in British culture at that time. We love championing British music and we're very proud of being British. We believe Britain has the most exciting, cutting-edge, forward-thinking, future-sounding music of all time. We create genres, we create scenes, we create movements, and the world follows. If you're a musician or producer and you're worried that AI is going to overtake your music, then work harder. Saul Milton (known as Chase) What drum and bass is about, and what hopefully our albums represent too, is unity. It's about all colours, creeds, races and religions coming together under one roof, having a good time and escaping the stresses of life. A lot of people worry that AI will replace artists. You don’t seem particularly worried about AI. Milton: The fear now, if there is a fear, is the complacency that it enables. Suddenly you can put in a prompt, type a few words and it spits something out. Whether it's good or not is another question, but the ease of it can squash creativity. Every change feels terrifying at the time. We went from vinyl and CDs to downloads, and from downloads to streaming. Every stage felt like the end of the world and every time people adapted. When we started, everything was samplers, synths and mixing desks. Then suddenly everything became digital. A lot of music didn't sound great at first because the technology was changing. Fast-forward 20 years and people have figured out how to make incredible-sounding records. I think we're still at the beginning of that process with AI. What can't AI replicate? Milton: Original ideas. Fundamentally, it's recycling ideas. It can make things polished, but it can't really think differently. Style is individuality. Will Kennard and Saul Milton of the English drum and bass duo Chase & Status pose for a photograph in London, Britain, September 30, 2026. REUTERS/Hannah McKay Kennard: The aim of the game now is to break out of that box and do something different and original. This album is partly a rebellion against our own generic selves. We could have made another record that sounded like our previous records, but that wouldn't have been progression. If AI becomes more powerful, what becomes the most valuable quality for an artist? Milton: Conviction. If you're a musician or producer and you're worried that AI is going to overtake your music, then work harder. Put more into the craft. Come at it from a different angle. If everyone's going left, go right. What do you hope people take away from Generic Everything? Milton: I hope people see it as an honest reflection of where Will and I are right now. We deliberately tried not to repeat ourselves. We didn't want to make another record that simply sounded like previous Chase & Status albums. The whole point was to challenge ourselves and avoid taking the easy route. I hope people listen to it from start to finish because that's becoming increasingly rare. Albums are still important to us. We spend a lot of time thinking about the order of the tracks and the journey they take you on. More than anything, I hope people can hear that we're trying new things. It isn't about chasing trends or following what's popular. It's about pushing ourselves creatively and seeing where that takes us. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: L'Ukraine dit que Starlink/Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à plus de 400 km/h
item.description: Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. Ces systèmes ont été perturbés pendant plus d'une semaine par des restrictions de service qui ont ralenti les connexions et affecté les opérations militaires de l'Ukraine face à la Russie. "Les systèmes de surveillance du ministère de la Défense enregistrent un retour à une vitesse normale de Starlink/Starshield. Nous enregistrons une vitesse supérieure à 400 km/h. La connexion est stable", a dit Evhenii Khmara à des journalistes. L'armée ukrainienne ne communique pas sur les vitesses maximales d'exploitation de ces réseaux et le ministère de la Défense n'a pas précisé si le service avait été pleinement rétabli. Les restrictions à l'utilisation de Starlink, signalées pour la première fois le 14 octobre, ont affaibli les capacités ukrainiennes d'interception des drones russes et perturbé les communications sur la ligne de front, ont dit les responsables ukrainiens. Selon diverses sources, les vitesses de connexion avaient été réduites à 160 km/h voire moins. Les problèmes de l'Ukraine avec le réseau Starlink, propriété de SpaceX, entreprise d'Elon Musk, sont apparus après l'annonce par le président américain Donald Trump d'un accord avec son homologue russe Vladimir Poutine sur la livraison par la Russie de diesel aux Etats-Unis et le blocage de nouvelles sanctions américaines contre Moscou. Donald Trump a simultanément exigé de l'Ukraine l'arrêt de ses bombardements contre les raffineries russes. Ni Elon Musk ni l'exécutif américain n'ont admis être à l'origine de ces restrictions frappant l'Ukraine et tous deux ont publiquement déclaré qu'une telle décision ne pouvait être prise que par l'autre partie. Reuters a rapporté que l'ordre de limiter l'exploitation de Starshield émanait de la Maison blanche.

item.title: France protests begin under heavy security as police seek to prevent fresh unrest
item.description: The interior minister mobilized 70,000 police nationwide for Saturday's demonstrations, 10,000 more than on October 17, when vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Alessandro Parodi
item.content:encoded: Demonstrators gathered in Paris and cities across France on Saturday under the watch of 70,000 police officers, as the government sought to prevent a repeat of the riots and looting that rocked the country [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last weekend"]. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 135 people had been arrested nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons. "We have to be ultra, ultra responsive. We have significant calls for disruption from political groups and quite simply from criminals," he told reporters. "It is going to be a long day." While the start of the main Paris march was peaceful, police fired tear gas at crowds in Lyon, France's third-largest city. The government has deployed 10,000 more police and gendarmes than on October 17, when protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services descended into some of the worst unrest France has seen in years. SHOPS, MUSEUMS SHUT Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. "There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. "Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans. The route for Paris' main demonstration was settled only after a legal battle triggered by a last-minute police order moving organisers away from the city centre towards the southeastern fringes of the capital. Police argued the original route passed through areas with a high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted last weekend. Leftist leaders said the late change was aimed at causing confusion and keeping people away. "Once again, those in power are creating disruption for the marches and impossible deadlines for organisations to reorganise themselves," said hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the crowds on the streets of Paris. FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of over-reacting, with soldiers dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees. "We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. "My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added. The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city. Tensions were heightened by a [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. "We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.

item.title: Ukraine says Starlink speed limits lifted after disruptions to military ops
item.description: Kyiv said Starshield connections were stable in overnight tests, with speed limits raised to above 400 kmph from 161 kmph in recent days, after disruptions to drone missions and military logistics ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Daryna Krasnolutska Ukraine said limits on the speed of its SpaceX Starlink terminal connections had been lifted in overnight testing, a move that may ease the latest tensions between Kyiv and Washington.  “The Defence Ministry’s monitoring systems are seeing the recovery of Starlink/Starshield speed; the connections are stable,” Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday. “It is another example when direct dialogue and the Ukrainian president’s firm stance at the highest level deliver results. And this result is important first and foremost for our front lines, our military, drone operations, logistics and communications,” Khmara told reporters.  Recent reduced operating speeds for Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, caught Ukrainian troops off-guard, disrupting some missions and undermining defence capabilities against Russian jet-powered drone barrages. Ukraine said it got no explanation from the US for the change, and that the throttling seemed deliberate.  The defence ministry on Saturday said Starshield was again working at speeds above 400 kilometers (248 miles) per hour after having been limited to about 161 km in recent days.  Relations between Ukraine and the US reached a new low after US President Donald Trump cut a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin this month under which Washington would refrain from further tightening sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow supplying limited volumes of diesel to the global market to curb rising prices. Speaking to Bloomberg News last weekend, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Moscow. He also said the US was delaying deliveries of crucial Patriot air defence interceptors used to defend Ukraine’s cities. The US also failed to share early warning alerts about Russian ballistic missiles attacking Ukraine several times, he said.  Trump said he didn’t order limits of speed for Starlink operation, but criticised Zelenskyy, saying the Ukrainian is more difficult to deal with than Putin.   The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump had spoken to SpaceX Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk, asking that he end restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine.

item.title: Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling
item.description: The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kyiv's defence minister said on Saturday, ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:

Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling

Reuters

24 October, 2026 03:00 pm IST

KYIV, Oct 24 (Reuters) – The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kyiv’s defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.

“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable,” Evhenii Khmara told reporters.

The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems’ maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.

Show Full Article

“Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal,” the ministry said.

The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said. Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.

Ukraine’s problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.

Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.

Trump said on Friday that if problems with access to Starlink communications systems in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out”.

(Reporting by Dan Peleschuk, writing by Yuliia DysaEditing by Ros Russell)
